By: ALTYDVRYSTAAT PRODUCTIONS | Delivery

Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Cart Blanche: The conflict in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado province has escalated dramatically in recent months. Are we dealing with a localized revolt, or a full fledged invasion by a extremi

Unique Selling Point:
Tonight we talk to experts with intimate knowledge of the region, its challenges as well as its war torn past.

Summary:
Since 2017, Islamist militants, some of which are reported to be affiliated with the Islamic State terror group, have been carrying out attacks against civilians and Mozambican armed forces. The violence has killed more than 1,000 people and displaced over 210,000 others, according to the United Nations. Is this an uprising or full blown war? And what influence will the conflict have on other countries in the region? Carte Blanche investigates.

Press Release:


The Ignored War: Islamic State in Southern Africa?

A dark shadow has stealthily crept over the dream-holiday destination of Cabo Delgado province in Northern Mozambique in the last three years. An estimated 1500 people have been killed and 200,000 displaced in skirmishes between security forces, civilians and the Islamist militant group Ansar al-Sunna. Carte Blanche investigates whether the insurgency marks the Islamic State gaining a foothold in Southern Africa, or whether it’s just local discontent exploited for extremist propaganda.

Producers: Hendrik Hancke & Niel van Deventer | Presenter: Derek Watts



Script:


Ignored War Script

V/O
Tropical Cabo Delgado province of Mozambique is known for its lush jungles, beautiful idyllic coastline and exclusive 30,000 dollar a night island hotels...but a rising tide of violence perpetrated by an Islamist militant group Ansar al-Sunna is infesting paradise.
Derek Link Over the last 3 years a dark shadow has fallen over this dream holiday destination. With what started as isolated skirmishes have escalated into more sophisticated battles with Ansar al sunna showing their capabilities in a major assault.

VO
Since July 2017 more than 1 500 people have died in Cabo Delgado and 200 000 have been displaced. 33-year old Maimuna Bakar is one of these people.
Maimuna Bakar We were well, we used to do business, the children studied everyday, but when the war started, there is nothing, no one does anything, nobody studies, no one does business, hunger, they destroyed Mocimboa, there is no-one there.

VO
At the height of its dominance, the Islamic State held about a third of Syria and 40 percent of Iraq. By 2017 it had lost 95 percent of its territory and IS and its radical Islamic views started trickling south into Africa. Kenia, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo became easy targets… Before long, Mozambique, and in particular Cabo Delgado, started to feel the brunt of the extremist expansion.

Maimuna Bakar I saw military men killed, houses burned, they even burned my house. I have nothing left.

VO
In Cabo Delgado IS found an unhappy population, ripe for radicalization and Ansar Al-Sunna was formed.

Jasmine Opperman
People are shouting islamic state left right and centre, but we need to understand the islamic state since the fall of the caliphate.

VO
Terrorism expert Jasmine Opperman says publishing claims made by the Islamic State on incidents of violence in Mozambique is playing right into the Islamic State’s hands. Opperman believes IS has lost their state and their leader and is looking for a foothold in another country in order to expand.

Jasmine Opperman
Africa has provided a lucrative opportunity for them to propagate their global expansion and that is central to their propaganda message. “We are still here, we are taking lead.”

VO
But propaganda or not, people are dying in Cabo Delgado.

At first, the insurgents focused their attention on isolated military, police and civilian targets.

But in August this year the situation changed dramatically when they conquered the strategically important harbor town, Mocimboa da Praia.

People fled the province to get out of harm’s way. Bakar and her family arrived in Pemba by sailboat - a harrowing trip that lasted five days.

Maimuna Bakar
We suffered from hunger. It wasn’t just us. Another boat was there. I saw three women who died of hunger and three children who died of hunger too. And we left them on the island.

VO
Gathered against the insurgents, are the Mozambican military, the police, and the airborne, private military company, Dyck Advisory Group, commanded by the retired Zimbabwean colonel, Lionel Dyck. … In the jungle, where uniforms and insignias are seldom visible, local residents live in constant fear.

Bacar Mussa
My brother, he was in the salt field...

VO
Before 72-year old Bacar Mussa fled to Pemba from Mahate, a village in Quissang-province, he lost everything. Including his brother.

Bacar Mussa
One day he saw a helicopter above him, then he left the salt field and ran to a shelter. Then he called our nephew to accompany him to an island called Pagombe. He went there and he died there.

Bacar blames his brother’s death squarely on the Dyck Advisory Group’s helicopters.
Col. Dyck did not want to go on camera - he agreed to speak to us telephonically.
Dyck says South Africa isn’t sending in military support and the Southern African Development Community hasn’t helped either, leaving Mozambique no other choice but to lean on the private security company for support.
“My guys would never kill a civilian on purpose, but people must remember IS always hides amongst civilians. In the fog of war it is impossible to operate with no civilian casualties, even though we work hard to avoid it.”
Jasmine Opperman Like a local said to me; there are three things we fear - the insurgents, the government security forces and the sound of choppers.

VO
In 2010 enormous liquid natural gas deposits were discovered in Cabo Delgado. The French oil company Total is one of the international players that has invested an estimated $60 billion in this operation. The gas is supposed to start flowing out of Mozambique by 2023.

Johann Smith
Cabo Delgado is one of the poorest provinces in Mozambique. They have the highest illiteracy rate of 64%.

VO
Risk analyst and former military man, Johann Smith, who has been living in Maputo for almost ten years, says with the discovery of natural gas, everything changed.

Johann Smith
It is the biggest direct foreign investment south of the Sahara ever. Indicative of the strategic importance of the source was the fact that none of the oil companies decided to declare force majeure or leave during Covid and the current security situation.

Derek link
With the discovery of rich gas deposits the villagers of Cabo de Gado expected their lifestyles to improve along with food security but what seems to have happened is just the opposite.

VO*
Martin Ewi, an analyst with the Institute for Security Studies, believes the people on the ground are not getting what is due to them.
He believes corruption and government mismanagement prevents money and service delivery from reaching its intended recipients - the citizens of Mozambique.

Martin Ewi
Derek: Certainly the riches aren’t filtering down much to the local population?
Most certainly it is not and that is the cause of the insurgency that we are seeing. You know, the locals trying to reclaim what they believe is theirs, trying to reclaim their own share of the riches.

V/O
Ewi believes this problem could’ve been resolved earlier.

Martin Ewi
If you want to address the problem on the ground you need to address the suffering of the people, the plight of the people, because it has gotten to the point where the people are blaming the government.

VO
What began in 2017, as a population dissatisfied with its government, and armed with pangas showing their discontent through violent action...has now evolved into a military force so sophisticated that in August this year, it sank a Mozambican naval interceptor boat.

Jasmine Opperman
They looted, they vandalised and acted with brutality against the locals.

V/O
The insurgents are not letting up on their campaign of terror against the villages... and they’re growing in sophistication.

Maimuna Bakar
The third time, they started causing destruction, kill, burn the houses. They took the children, many, many children, young boys, girls between 15 and 20 years old, they took them, the children too.They even took my cousin’s child to the bush.

Jasmine Opperman
I would easily say at this point in time 80% of villages have either been attacked, destroyed by arson and deserted.There is simply nothing left. Mocimboa da Praia and the area around it, it’s a no man’s land.

DEREK LINK
One of the major concerns is how far south the conflict could eventually spread. Could it extend to popular destinations like Vilanquilos or all the way to Ponto d’Ouro?

Jasmine Opperman
Pushing down further south has not shown its face yet. My fear is that we are gonna walk into a stage of covert organised cells, executing attacks beyond the current areas that we are seeing violence taking place.

VO
But Smith believes that although Pemba would be the logical next target for the insurgents, he doubts if they have the capabilities to capture and keep the city.

Johann Smith
Incidents of terror is not far-fetched because we have seen over recent times a lot more arrests have been made within Pemba of supposed insurgents. And it is a worrying thing. And that it could spread further south is quite true.

VO
But perhaps more concerning is that many of the radicals who were detained, have been released. Smith insists that the situation in Cabo Delgado is a regional problem and must be dealt with by the Southern African Development Community, or SADC.

Johann Smith
From a strategic point of view there is no way that we can let it be. And it must be dealt with in SADC. And the SADC security organ should have long ago decided on a strategy.

Martin Ewi
If terrorism happens in your backyard your neighbours should be concerned. Something has to be done to prevent what is happening in Northern Mozambique from spreading to other countries

Derek link:
Which leaves a question that affects all of us in South Africa; should our military get actively involved, and if so, what are the possible repercussions?

Martin Ewi We are not saying South Africa should intervene, we are saying South Africa should use the resources that it has to support Mozambique.

VO
Ewi believes that by intervening through the auspices of SADC it will remove the extremists focus on South Africa.

Martin Ewi
The situation in Cabo DelGado is getting worse every day and each day that we wait people are dying, people are losing their livelihoods. And how many people do we want to lose their livelihoods, how many people do we want to die before we take definitive action against those who are perpetrating this act.

Bacar Mussa
I would like for the war to finish and I would go back there. I live alone here. I would like it there. This is the time to prepare the salt fields. It is the time when I prepare the salt fields, to have salt, to earn, to have money, to eat. This is the time. Now I am isolated here. I am scared to go back there.



PROMO 1 11” * The once idyllic tourist paradise of Cabo Delgado in Mozambique lies in ruins after continued attacks by radical insurgents have turned the region into a warzone.


PROMO 2 11” Once a tourism hotspot, now a hotspot for terrorists. We take you inside Mozambique’s Cabo Delgado province where violent terrorists continue to wage ...


PROMO 3 11” Once a picture perfect tropical paradise, Cabo Delgado province of Mozambique is now a shadow of its former self as violent insurgents stalk what’s left of this tourism favourite.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Cart Blanche: The conflict in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado province has escalated dramatically in recent months. Are we dealing with a localized revolt, or a full fledged invasion by a extremi
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Tonight we talk to experts with intimate knowledge of the region, its challenges as well as its war torn past.
metadata.Summary: Since 2017, Islamist militants, some of which are reported to be affiliated with the Islamic State terror group, have been carrying out attacks against civilians and Mozambican armed forces. The violence has killed more than 1,000 people and displaced over 210,000 others, according to the United Nations. Is this an uprising or full blown war? And what influence will the conflict have on other countries in the region? Carte Blanche investigates.
